The match mattered to her father the way certain matches mattered to certain men, which is to say more than he would admit in words. But it mattered to Amelia differently, and she had been keeping that quietly to herself all week: she had a presentiment, unfounded and specific, that this tournament would be the one where the game she loved and the game her father loved finally became visibly two different games, and she wanted to be watching when it happened.

"It's forty-eight teams this time," Daniyal said, leaning forward over the shared plate of nachos. "Some people at school were saying it's still thirty-two."

"It's thirty-two," her father said, not looking away from the screen. "It's been thirty-two since the nineties."

"You're both wrong," Sofie said mildly. "It's forty-eight, but that's not the interesting part. It's three countries hosting. Canada, Mexico, us." She tore another strip off the napkin. "That's never happened before either."

Amelia's father turned from the screen with the slow, saturnine attention he reserved for people contradicting him in public. "Three countries," he repeated, as though tasting something suspicious.

"That's the whole thing," Sofie said. "First time with forty-eight teams, first time with three hosts. It's on the poster in the metro station."

He grunted and returned to the game, where a midfielder had just given the ball away in his own third, and he lambasted the man with a fluency Amelia had inherited in diluted form, whispering a single critical word into her soda.

Before halftime, her brother knocked over his lemonade reaching across Daniyal for a nacho, and while the waitress brought a towel and her mother apologized twice for no reason, Amelia caught Sofie checking her phone under the table, turning it face down, checking it again. Sofie's want was no secret exactly, just undiscussed: her brother had moved out in March after a fight whose contents Sofie never gave, and she monitored her phone the way you monitor a weather radar when a storm might be tracking toward you.

At halftime the restaurant filled and the noise rose, and Amelia went with Daniyal to the counter to order more fries. On the way back he said, low, "Your dad looked at me like I'd insulted his mother over the team count."

"He'll come around. He just doesn't like learning things from a poster."

"Is it actually true, though? You looked it up?"

"Last night," Amelia said. "For an hour. I kept finding the same two things and nothing else." She balanced the fries along her forearm. "It's strange. The whole structure changed, and it's like nobody agrees on whether that makes it a bigger thing or a worse thing. Sofie thinks bigger. My dad thinks worse, he just hasn't said it yet."

When they sat down, Sofie slid her phone across the table toward Amelia, screen up. A message from her brother, sent that morning, that she had evidently read forty times: "Watching the game at Finnegan's if your family wants company. Door's open either way. R." Below it sat her draft reply, unsent, the cursor blinking after the word "Maybe."

"You don't have to show me that," Amelia said.

"I know. I wanted someone to look at it who wasn't inside it." Sofie's eyes were steady. "Is maybe the right answer?"

Amelia thought of her father, certain for twenty years and wrong in one sentence. She thought of the tournament itself, three nations sharing a thing that had always belonged to one. "Maybe is honest," she said. "Maybe is better than yes when you're not sure. Send it and see what he says back. You can decide from there."

Sofie typed for a moment, then set the phone down between them, face up this time, and picked up a fry.

The second half began with a goal inside four minutes, and the restaurant erupted, and her father was on his feet with his arms up, shouting the player's name, all his earlier certainty dissolved in pure noise. Amelia watched Sofie's phone light up on the table between the nacho plate and the lemonade-stained napkins, vibrating once, twice, a reply arriving from somewhere across the city where another screen was showing the same game.

"Aren't you going to look?" Amelia said.

"In a minute," Sofie said, and took a breath, and picked it up.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius (40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly.
story:
Sebastian stood in his grandfather's kitchen on the first Sunday of the month with a legal pad and three grocery flyers spread across the counter. His grandfather had agreed, with some astonishment, that Sebastian would take over the cooking until the end of summer. The deal had been his mother's idea, delivered over the phone in the tone she reserved for arrangements already decided: he would learn to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients, and cook them in batches on Sundays so that his grandfather, who had been living on crackers and tinned soup since the operation, would eat something with a vegetable in it.

The planning took longer than he expected. He wrote out seven dinners, cross-checked them against what was on sale, and discovered that a chicken could appear as roast, as curry, and as soup without anyone complaining, provided the side dishes rotated. He made a list organized by aisle, then reorganized it by the order in which items would spoil, because he'd read somewhere that this mattered, though he couldn't have said why. At the store he bought too much of everything anyway. His grandfather's fridge, when he got the bags home, smelled of old butter and held a single jar of pickles at eye level, like an exhibit.

Jordan came by on the second Sunday, ostensibly to help, and stood at the doorway of the kitchen watching Sebastian brown beef in the big enamel pot. "You're like a person in a commercial," Jordan said. "A person in a commercial for a life nobody has." Sebastian told him about the danger zone, which he'd looked up the night before after wondering how long the cooked chili could sit out while the batches cooled. "The USDA calls four to sixty degrees Celsius, that's forty to one forty Fahrenheit, the danger zone. That's where bacteria in food multiply rapidly." Jordan pulled a stool over to the counter and asked whether that was why his mother screamed at people who thawed chicken on the counter, and Sebastian said probably, yes, and portioned the chili into containers with a ladle, steam rising off them and fogging the window over the sink.

The mistake happened the third week. His grandfather had wanted to sit outside while the sauce simmered, and they sat on the porch until dark, the neighbor Ms. Chan watering her tomatoes across the fence and telling a story about a cousin who had once driven a delivery truck through the front of a bakery in Queens. When Sebastian finally went in, the pot of chili was still on the stove, the burner off, the lid on, the kitchen warm and sweet-smelling with cumin. It was nearly eleven. He was tired, and the pot was heavy, and he told himself he'd deal with it in the morning, and went up to bed.

In the morning the pot was sitting exactly where he'd left it, skin formed on the surface, and Abraham was at the table eating cereal. Abraham had started showing up on Mondays because word had gotten around that there was food. He looked at the pot, then at Sebastian, and said, "How long has that been out?" Sebastian said since about eleven. Abraham set his spoon down. "My dad does food safety for a living. He won't even leave pizza out overnight." Sebastian stood there with his hand on the lid, doing the arithmetic: eight hours, well within the range, all night in the warm kitchen, somewhere in that span between four and sixty degrees where everything multiplied so fast it had been given its own name.

He carried the pot to the sink and poured it out, and the chili went down the drain in a slow brown rope, and he scraped the skin and the last of it into the bin and washed the pot in water so hot it sensitized his wrists, going pink and then numb, so that he had to grip the sponge carefully for the last of the scrubbing. It was, he thought, a strange kind of education, the kind where the tuition was five pounds of beef and an evening of chopping, and where the lesson landed not when he read the numbers on the website but when the food itself slid away from him under the tap.

Afterward he sat with his grandfather on the porch and told him the whole sequence, the cooling, the porch, the morning, the drain. His grandfather listened with his hands folded on his knee. "In my day we left things out all the time," he said. "Your grandmother left soup out overnight her whole life and lived to eighty-one." Sebastian said that plenty of people got away with it and plenty didn't, and there was no way to know which kind of night this one had been, so the only safe assumption was the bad one. His grandfather considered this. "You've become quite the scientist," he said, in a tone that Sebastian couldn't entirely read, whether it was approval or the mild disappointment of an old misanthrope watching another young person surrender to rules.

They didn't agree about it, and Sebastian noticed that he didn't fully agree with himself. The atavistic part of him, the part that had watched his grandmother cool pies on the windowsill, thought the whole business was a little hysterical. The part of him that had poured eight hours of work down the drain thought the numbers were simply true whether you liked them or not. He told his grandfather he'd cook a fresh batch that afternoon, smaller this time, and that from now on the containers would go straight into the fridge, lids off, in the cold basement where they'd cool fast, before anything could multiply in that warm belt in between.

That evening the new chili simmered, and Ms. Chan called over the fence that it smelled better than anything on the street, and Abraham arrived at the door without being invited, holding a loaf of bread like a ticket. Sebastian ladled out four bowls and set the pot, uncovered, on the cold porch rail, where the night air was already dropping toward ten degrees, and he checked the thermometer he'd bought that afternoon, the one with the little red dial, and pressed it against the side of the pot. "Forty-two," he said. "Getting there."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
Naomi's birthday fell on the fourth of November, which meant that for exactly one day she had been eighteen, and for exactly one day the election belonged to her. She had been planning the moment since September, when she'd updated her registration at the DMV with a clerk who typed her information without looking up, and she'd imagined it since she was small, standing beside her mother at the fire station, watching people disappear behind the curtain of the old lever machines. Now it was a Tuesday morning, and the polls closed at eight that night, and she could not find her confirmation email anywhere in the house.

"Did you see a letter from the county?" she asked her mother, who was on her hands and knees under the kitchen table retrieving a dropped pen cap. Her mother had not. Naomi searched her desk, the drawer where the good pens went to die, the folder labeled IMPORTANT that contained a receipt for bike repairs and nothing else. Her registration, she was fairly sure, had gone through. She remembered the clerk's screen, the little chime. But fairly sure, she was beginning to understand, was not the same as sure, and sure was the only thing the county would accept.

She texted Ely, who had voted at seven in the morning like a person who enjoys being first in line for anything. "did they check ur name on a list," she typed, and Ely sent back a photo of the I Voted sticker arranged artfully on a sociology textbook. Not helpful. Jaime was more practical: "just go. bring id and the dmv receipt if u have it. the worst thing they can say is no." This was, Naomi thought, exactly the kind of reassurance Jaime specialized in, optimistic and technically incomplete, because the worst thing they could say was no to her, specifically, on the one day her vote was possible at all.

The community hall was four blocks away, in the gymnasium with the basketball hoops winched up to the ceiling and the banners from 1998 still hanging. At the check-in table an older woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain ran a finger down the printed list, once, then again, then a third time with the assistance of a second poll worker, a young man in a hoodie under his official lanyard. "Yusuf, N. through Zabala," the woman said, mostly to herself. Naomi watched her own absence travel down the page. It was a strange feeling, being legally real and alphabetically nowhere.

"There's no Naomi Yusuf," the woman said at last, apologetically, as though she had misplaced her personally. "It happens sometimes with a new registration. But you can still vote today."

"How?" Naomi asked, and heard in her own voice an eagerness she hadn't intended to show.

"You can cast a provisional ballot," the young man said. "It's sealed in an envelope with your info on it, and it counts only once the officials confirm you're eligible." He said it briskly, the way a cashier recites a return policy, and pulled a cream-colored envelope from a drawer, and Naomi understood that her morning of panic had, all along, had a procedure attached to it, a form designed precisely for people the list had failed.

She filled it out at a table near the water fountains, printing carefully, and while she printed she thought about Ms. Nair, her eleventh-grade civics teacher, who had once delivered a whole peroration on the franchise, leaning against the whiteboard, growing more pugnacious with every sentence about people who fought and bled for the right she was now exercising with a golf pencil. Naomi had rolled her eyes at sixteen. She was not rolling them now, holding her sealed envelope like something that might still turn out to be nothing. That was the part Ms. Nair hadn't covered: that a ballot could be conditional. That you could do everything right, arrive on time, sign every line, and still leave carrying a maybe.

Walking home through the parked cars and the leaf piles, she called Ely, who had a theory, as Ely always did, that the DMV clerk had monetized the wait times somehow and cut corners on the data entry, a theory Naomi found implausible and somehow comforting. She called the county office, waited on hold past the point of dignity, and gave a clerk her name and birthday and address. There was a pause, keyboard sounds, another pause. "I can see the application," the clerk said. "I can't tell you over the phone whether it processed. You'll get a notice about the provisional within, I want to say, a couple of weeks."

"Whether it counted," Naomi said slowly, tasting the shape of it, "I won't know for weeks."

"That's right."

At home the kitchen smelled like onions her mother had started for no dish in particular. "Well?" her mother asked, turning. Naomi put the stub with the toll-free number on the counter between them and slid it forward like a playing card. "It's called a provisional ballot," she said. "They'll open it if they can confirm I'm real, and they'll tell me by mail." Her mother picked up the stub, read it twice, and set it down again with the careful touch she used for things that were Naomi's and not hers. Outside, a car went by with a flag still flapping from the window, hours past the point where flags did any good. Naomi put water on for tea and sat down across from the stub, waiting with it.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and cold coffee, and Angelina had spread her chemistry notes across the workbench because the house was too loud and the library closed at nine. Her father's old tarp hung over the lawnmower in the corner like something sleeping. She had a test in two days on equilibrium, and she did not understand it, and the not-understanding had begun to feel physical, a tightness behind her eyes.

Malek arrived on his bike with a plastic bag of energy drinks and no apology for being twenty minutes late. He set his phone on the bench, found a page of practice problems, and read the first one aloud in a flat voice. "A reaction at equilibrium is cooled. Which way does it shift?"

"Wrong way," Angelina said. "It goes back toward the reactants. Or forward. I genuinely don't know, that's the problem."

Imogen came through the side door before he could answer, holding her own notebook against her chest the way she held everything, carefully. She was the one who had gotten them into this, because Ms. García had pulled her aside after class and said the three of them could pull their grades up together if they actually tried, and Imogen took that kind of thing as a kind of vow. She sat on an overturned bucket and uncapped a pen. "Okay, so, exothermic reactions release heat. Heat is a product. If you cool it, you take away product, so it makes more."

Malek said the principle was named after some French guy, which Angelina already knew, because she had looked him up the week before at the science museum, standing in front of a panel while her mother wandered toward the planetarium. She had found his name there and searched it on her phone in the dim light. "The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier," she said, reciting it almost exactly as the museum had printed it, "and he stated it in 1884." She liked the way the sentence held together, a whole fact she could stand on.

"But what does he have to do with my answer?" Malek asked.

"Nothing. That's the point." Angelina pulled her knees up onto the stool. "It's not his fault I don't get it. He just noticed that systems push back. You change something, the system shifts to undo the change." She paused. "I think."

Imogen worked a problem in silence, her pen moving in small laconic strokes, few marks, no crossing out, as if she had decided the answer before she touched the paper. Angelina watched her and felt the familiar split in herself: the part that wanted to memorize the rules, cold means this, pressure means that, and the part that wanted to know why, which was slower and had failed her on the last test. Her older sister called that second part a waste of time. Her sister was in business school now and spoke of efficiency the way other people spoke of weather.

Ms. García lived three doors down, and she appeared in the driveway at ten, walking her dog, and knocked on the open garage door when she saw the light. She did not come in. She asked what they were studying, and Angelina told her, bracing for a lecture, but Ms. García only said, "Try the water one. Ice and liquid water at zero degrees. What happens if you add heat?" The dog pulled at its leash and she went on down the street, and Angelina stood in the doorway watching her go, annoyed and grateful in the same breath.

Back at the bench, they tried it. Malek said the ice would melt, obviously. Imogen said so it shifts toward the side that uses up the heat, the liquid side. Angelina wrote it down and then, without planning to, wrote underneath it: the system absorbs what you force on it, or resists it, and you can read the shift off the temperature. She thought of her sister's word for close reading, hermeneutics, which she had looked up months ago and never used aloud, and thought that this was its own kind of reading, that the reaction was a text and the conditions were the questions you brought to it. She did not say that out loud. Some things you write in the margin and keep.

"Again," she said, and turned the page. "This time you cool it."

Malek cracked an energy drink and set it sweating on the bench beside her notes. Imogen drew two boxes and an arrow between them. Somewhere outside a car door slammed, and the fluorescent tube overhead buzzed once and steadied. Angelina put her pen to the paper and waited to see which way she believed it would go.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
Isla arrived at the community studio first, as she always did, and claimed the long table by the window because its light was honest. Her portfolio was due in nine days, and the piece she had promised the admissions panel was a portrait of her grandmother, painted in colors that no tube contained: a particular orange, the orange of a paper lantern at the end of a night market street, half memory and half invention. She had a photograph pinned to the easel and a palette knife in her hand and forty minutes before Sana and Kayne showed up.

She began with cadmium yellow and added red, a little at a time, testing each mixture on scrap paper. Too pale. She added more red. Too rusty. She added white to lift it, then more yellow to warm it again, then a thread of magenta because the photograph, when she squinted, held something pink in it. The color on her knife grew complicated, and every addition seemed to take the mixture further from what she wanted rather than closer.

"Trying to propitiate the paint gods?" Sana said, dropping her bag on the stool beside her. Sana was glazing mugs for her mother's birthday, a project she'd started three weeks ago and abandoned twice, and she wanted, more than anything she said out loud, for her mother to keep this one instead of putting it in the cupboard with the others, the ones she called too nice to use.

"I keep adding and it keeps getting worse," Isla said. "Look at this. It was almost right four mixtures ago, and now it's just..." She held up the scrap. The swatch had gone the color of wet cardboard.

Kayne leaned over from the opposite side of the table, where he was supposed to be finishing a canvas for his own application but had spent twenty minutes sketching a politician from the news instead, all sharp suit and pointing finger. "That's a demagogue," Sana said, tapping the sketch. "He's on again about closing the community centers. This one, actually. This studio." Kayne shrugged and said that was the point, that he wanted the portfolio piece to be about what was being taken, and Isla felt something cold move through her, because she hadn't known the center was on any list at all.

Ms. Suryanto came around with the coffee she was forever carrying and paused at Isla's scrap paper. She didn't lecture. She only said, "Show me what you've mixed," and looked at the palette, at the eight or nine pigments smeared there, and then said, "Try starting over with two," and walked away to help a man at the far table who was making a poster for a food drive, letters bold enough to read from the street.

Isla scraped her palette almost clean and thought about it while she worked. Every pigment she'd added was absorbing something, she realized, that was what pigment did, it swallowed part of the light, so the more of them she piled together the less light any of it could give back. Mixing paint wasn't like mixing light at all. It was subtractive. That was why her lantern orange kept sinking toward brown: she had been asking a stack of pigments to be brighter when every layer she added was taking more away. Two colors, a warm yellow and the right red, and she would have to accept whatever the photograph's pink had to be left out.

She mixed yellow and red and nothing else, and there on the scrap paper, on the sixth try, was the lantern, close enough that her chest hurt. She turned to tell Sana and found Sana holding a mug with a hairline crack running down from the rim, one of the earlier firings, and Kayne holding the studio's donation jar, which was nearly empty. "They said the center's been running destitute for a year," Kayne said quietly. "That's why it's on the list. They said at the meeting."

Sana set the cracked mug down in front of her mother's unfinished one, so the two sat rim to rim, and said, "Then mine's staying out where people can see it, cracked or not." Isla looked at her grandmother's face taking shape on the canvas, at the orange she had almost lost four mixtures ago and would lose again the moment she tried to make it perfect, and she picked up the brush and made the first stroke before the light moved.

"Just tell me one thing," Kayne said, still holding the jar. "If we pass this around at the exhibition, do you think anyone actually puts money in these things?"

Isla dipped the brush again, watching the red bleed into the yellow on the canvas. "Put it next to my grandmother," she said. "People stop for her."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The pool was quiet before six, its water flat under the long lights, and Mathis stood at the shallow end holding a clipboard he had not asked for. Ms. Whitaker had given it to him on Tuesday, after the doctor's appointment, and told him he was the record keeper now. On the clipboard was the protocol sheet for Angeline, who had hit her head on the wall during a turn three weeks ago.

The sheet had stages. Stage one was rest, no practice, no screens after dinner. Stage two was light activity, walking to school, easy stretching. Stage three was sport-specific exercise without risk of contact, and that was where Angeline was now, and that was the stage Mathis was supposed to watch. You moved up only while you stayed free of symptoms. If symptoms came back, you went down a stage and started again from there. It was written on the sheet in Ms. Whitaker's small even handwriting, and Mathis had read it so many times he could recite it in the shower.

Angeline came in at six with her bag over one shoulder and her hair already in a cap. Haroon was already in the water, warming up for the medley relay, and he lifted a hand out of the lane to wave. Angeline waved back and dropped her bag on the bench.

"Full practice today?" she said. She said it lightly, the way you ask about the weather.

"Stage three," Mathis said. "Kicking with a board, no flip turns, twenty minutes, then we see."

She looked at the water. "I did twenty minutes Tuesday with no problem."

"Then today should be easy."

He knew what she wanted. He wanted it too, honestly. The regional meet was in four weeks and the relay team had a real shot at finals, but only with Angeline swimming backstroke, because the boy who would otherwise take her leg, a quiet sophomore, was three seconds slower, and three seconds was the difference between a podium and nothing. Mathis had done that arithmetic many times, usually at night.

She kicked her twenty minutes, face down, board out front, and she looked fine. At the wall she stopped and held the gutter, and then she closed her eyes for a second too long.

"Headache?" Mathis said.

"I slept badly. That's all."

"Angeline."

"It's a two out of ten. The sheet says I have to tell you if it's back. It's back." She said it flatly, the way you report a time. Then she pulled herself out and sat on the edge with her legs in the water, and the water kept moving around her ankles after she had gone still.

Mathis looked at the clipboard. The rule was plain. She had to go back a stage, to light activity, and work up again from there, moving forward only while she stayed free of symptoms. He had not made the rule and he could not change it, and standing there he understood that being the one with the clipboard meant the rule arrived through him, wearing his voice.

"You're stepping back," he said. "Stage two. Light stuff. We try again when you're clear."

"For how long?"

"As long as it takes."

She nodded once. Haroon had stopped at the far end and was watching them over the lane rope, and Mathis could tell from his face that he had done the arithmetic too. Haroon climbed out and came over, dripping, and stood beside Angeline without saying anything for a while, which was his way of forestalling an argument he could not win.

That night Mathis sat at the kitchen table with his father, who was reading a review article about stress adaptation in rice, because that was his job, and who looked up when Mathis said he didn't know if he'd done the right thing.

"Explain it," his father said.

Mathis explained the stages, the steps upward, the rule about symptoms. His father listened the way he listened to data. "So the rule isn't about the meet," he said. "The rule is about her brain. The meet is your problem, not the rule's."

"I want the podium," Mathis said. "I'm allowed to want it."

"Of course. You just aren't allowed to want it more than she is allowed to be well." His father went back to his paper, and Mathis sat with that for a while, feeling melancholic in a way he couldn't quite locate, the way you feel at the end of a summer evening when nothing bad has happened yet.

The next two weeks, Angeline walked the track with Mathis in the mornings, stage two, easy movement, and she talked about her classes and he talked about his, and neither of them talked about the relay, which stood between them like furniture in a dark room. He caught himself watching her face for the squint that meant the headache, and he caught himself, worse, hoping sometimes not to see it, and he was honest enough with himself to know which hope was which. Wanting her healthy and wanting her fast were two different things, and he could hold both, but only if he kept them in separate hands.

On the Thursday of the second week she came to the pool at six and said, "Nothing for five days. Not one." Stage three again, kicking with the board, and she swam her twenty minutes clean, and then her twenty minutes again, and the week after that she did flip turns, and the week after that she raced Haroon in the shallow end and lost and laughed about it.

The night before the regional meet, she found Mathis folding towels in the equipment room.

"I was angry at you," she said. "For about four days. I thought you were being careful with me like I was something that would break."

"And now?"

"Now I think you were being careful with the rule, and I just happened to be attached to it." She picked up a stack of towels and put it on the shelf where it went. "Genotype versus phenotype, my bio teacher would say. You were managing the condition, not the person."

Mathis laughed. "I don't think that's what those words mean."

"Close enough." She shoved the last towel into his hands. "Six a.m. Warm-up. Don't be late."

He wasn't. He stood at the blocks with the clipboard under his arm while she stepped up, fixed her goggles, and set her toes over the edge.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906.
story:
I told everyone I didn't care about the paper, which was mostly true, and I told myself the rest until it fit. Ten percent of our grade, Mr. Ahmadi had said, holding up a photocopied page like a relic. An argument, footnotes, a bibliography, all in one citation style, all due Monday. My mother had shipped me to my grandmother's house for the weekend because our apartment was being repainted, which meant I would write it alone, at a dining table that smelled of lemon polish, under a portrait of my grandfather I had never met.

I had chosen my topic on the bus without reading anything, which is a thing you can do and still feel decisive. School uniforms improve behaviour: that was my thesis, and I had three sources from a quick search that seemed to agree with me. On Friday night I spread them across the table beside my grandmother's dish of peppermints and wrote two paragraphs of pure confidence. When Elle texted to ask how mine was going, I said nearly done. That was not true in any measurable way, but it felt true, and I have a gift for stopping the audit there.

Saturday morning, Rowan called. He was doing the same topic from the opposite side, uniforms as a way of stigmatize nothing but poverty, he said, marking kids who couldn't afford replacements, teaching everyone to read class off a collar. "Read the turnover study," he said. "The 2010 one, from the urban district. Then tell me your side survives it." I said I would, hung up, and did not open it for an hour. I ate a peppermint instead. Confidence, I've found, keeps better if you don't check the ingredients.

The study broke my paper in two. Suspension rates barely moved; attendance dipped; a majority of students surveyed called the uniforms a visceral reminder of being watched, though those weren't the researchers' words, they were Rowan's paraphrase in the margins of the PDF he'd sent. My three agreeing sources turned out to be opinion columns, one of them written by a uniform company's apologist, which I discovered when I followed the author's name down the page to the line about his consulting work. I sat at my grandmother's table with my head in my hands, and the portrait of my grandfather looked down at me like a man who had seen this kind of collapse before.

My grandmother found me there and asked what was wrong, and I told her, badly, that a rulebook I'd never read was ruining my weekend. She laughed and said her father had complaints about that book too. "The Chicago Manual of Style," she said. "Notes at the bottom of the page, bibliography at the end, everything accounted for. It was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906." She tapped the table. "Older than your great-grandparents, and still telling people where the commas go." I checked, because I check nothing my grandmother says out of love and everything out of habit, and she was right, all of it, the press, the year, the system. A book that old, still holding, while my argument hadn't survived a Saturday.

So I started over, and this is where I stopped trusting my own account of myself, because I'd been telling a story all weekend about a boy who didn't care, and here was a boy cross-referencing at ten at night, building footnotes line by line, number after number, caring with a violence I hadn't planned on. I kept Rowan's study and my broken columns and a third thing I found myself: a district where attendance rose, where students reported feeling safer, where the uniform had worked. I wrote a paper that said both, that the evidence was mixed and the honest position sat between my confidence and Rowan's, and that which side you fell on depended on whether you counted feeling watched as order or as harm. In the last footnote I flagged the one thing I couldn't resolve: whether safety reported in a survey is safety at all.

Sunday night I called Rowan and read him my conclusion. He was quiet long enough that I heard his television in the background.

"You flipped," he said.

"I stayed. You flipped me partway, the data flipped me the rest."

"So we agree now."

"No. I'm saying you're sixty percent right."

He laughed, and it didn't sound like losing to either of us. Monday morning I handed it in, fourteen pages, a bibliography in perfect order, and watched Mr. Ahmadi flip straight to the footnotes, his pen hovering, finding nothing to fix. He looked up at me over the page, then back down, and drew a slow circle around my final paragraph without writing a word beside it.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
Gavin had shared the video before dinner, and by the time he'd finished washing up it had four hundred reposts. A warehouse, supposedly outside Kyiv, full of aid boxes being relabeled and resealed. The caption said it had been filmed last week. His thumb had moved before the rest of him caught up, and now the thing sat in his feed like a stone dropped in a pond, rings still spreading.

Samy had messaged him twice. "did u see where this came from?" was the first. The second was just a link to a fact-checking site with a yellow banner that said the footage was under review. Gavin stared at that banner through half of a documentary his father had put on, and then went upstairs.

He'd been at his mother's office on Thursday, filling time in a corner chair while she finished a call. A colleague of hers, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, had been clicking through newsroom tools at the next desk, and Gavin had watched her drop a video into a small panel in the corner of her browser. Frames had bloomed across the screen like a contact sheet. When he'd leaned over to ask, she'd said, "InVID-WeVerify," as if that were the whole answer. "It splits a video into key frames so you can reverse-search them." His mother had added that the project behind it was funded by the European Union, in the tone she used for things she considered unimpeachably dull, and the woman had laughed and said a lot of verification tools came out of that funding.

Gavin sat on his bed now and typed the name into the plugin store. It installed with a small camera icon. He pulled the warehouse video's link, pasted it, and pressed the magnifier. The progress bar crawled, and then the screen filled with pale thumbnails: a hand sealing a box, a stack of pallets, a corridor between shelves, a face half-turned toward the lens. Key frames, he realized, each one a doorway.

He right-clicked the corridor shot and searched it. The results loaded slowly, and he caught himself holding his breath, which felt absurd, and he kept holding it anyway. The top hit was a news article from two years before the caption's claimed date. The second hit was a stock footage library. The third was a discussion thread where someone had already done exactly what he was doing and pasted the verdict: old footage, wrong location, wrong year.

He sat back. The honest part was that the fact-checking site had said "under review," not "false." Some commenters insisted the relabeling happened at other warehouses, that exposing one fake didn't disprove every claim. Gavin couldn't rule that out, and he was wary of the opposite trap, the blase shrug that said nothing online was real and so nothing required his attention. The footage was old; that much was solid. What it meant about the wider story stayed open, and he would have to be honest about that too.

He typed a reply to Samy: "it's recycled. two years old. ran the frames through InVID-WeVerify, the EU-funded thing that splits videos into key frames you can reverse-search." He posted it as a follow-up to his original repost, then spent ten minutes composing a second message, deleting drafts that sounded like a lecture and drafts that sounded like an apology for a crime. He settled on: "I should have checked before posting. The video's from 2023, not last week. Deleting my repost."

Deleting felt strangely physical, like pulling a thread from a sweater and hoping the whole thing didn't unravel. The repost vanished. The replies to it did not; a few people had already quoted him, one saying "so it's fake?? source?" and another who seemed to impugn his motives, suggesting he'd shared it deliberately to make the aid campaign look bad and was now covering himself. He read that one twice. His first instinct was to defend himself at length, and his second was to leave it, because a long defense would only feed the thread, and because he wasn't entirely sure how much of his quickness to share had been carelessness and how much had been wanting the likes.

Haley, who was in his media studies class and had a habit of arriving at conclusions from angles nobody else had considered, messaged him a few minutes later. "funny how the fake spread faster than your correction," she wrote. "like the correction doesn't have the same shape. it's not as shareable. the phenomenology of it is different." He had to look up phenomenology, and even the dictionary left it soft at the edges, something about how a thing is experienced rather than what it is. The fake was experienced as a revelation; the correction was experienced as homework.

He thought about that while the evening thinned outside his window. One repost deleted, one source checked, one tool learned. It wasn't nothing, and it wasn't enough, and he couldn't yet say which of those facts mattered more. Tomorrow he'd show Samy how the plugin worked, frame by frame, so the checking could spread even if the correction didn't.

Downstairs his mother called something about tea. He left the plugin icon glowing in the browser, went to the stairs, and called back, "Two sugars," and waited for the small ritual sound of the spoon against the cup.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
story:
Joshua had walked the nature trail behind the school maybe forty times, but he had never once run it, and he had never once thought about his legs while doing either. Today he was doing both, because on Monday he had written "ATP comes from the mitochondria" on a quiz and Ms. Kang had circled it and written, in her small patient hand, that this was like saying bread comes from a bakery. The retake was Thursday. Ireland claimed the trail loop was exactly a mile and a half, which meant nothing to Joshua except that it was long enough to hurt.

They started easy, gravel crunching, the woods opening onto a mowed strip along a fence line. Ireland ran like someone who had done this before, arms loose, breathing through his nose. Joshua ran like someone remembering a list: glucose, then glycolysis, then pyruvate, then the mitochondria, then ATP, like beads on a string he kept dropping. "You're thinking out loud," Ireland said without turning his head. "Sorry." "It's fine. It's better than when you were humming."

The list was not the problem, or not all of it. The problem was that the list had a shape he couldn't see. Why would a cell bother splitting glucose at all if it only got two ATP out of it, when the mitochondria later made so many more? He had tried to codify it that night, writing rules in his notebook, numbered steps with arrows, and the arrows looked official and told him nothing. Ms. Kang had said something in class about the split being ancient, older than oxygen, but he hadn't written it down because it hadn't sounded like something that would be on a quiz.

At the fence line the trail dipped through a farm field, knee-high grass, and Ireland said, "Race you to the gate," and was gone before the sentence ended. Joshua went after him. The grass grabbed at his shoes. Somewhere in the middle of the field his thighs began to burn, a heat that sharpened into a specific ache, and his breath went ragged and shallow and his pace collapsed to something barely faster than walking. Ireland beat him by twenty meters and jogged back, hands on his hips, grinning. "You died out there." "My legs just stopped," Joshua said, bent over. "They didn't stop. They slowed down."

Isabelle was sitting on the bottom rail of the gate, waiting for them, a water bottle sweating in her hand. She had come out to sketch for an art portfolio and had watched the whole race from the shade of a hickory. She watched Joshua now, his hands braced on his knees, and she thought about how deliberate he looked even in pain, like someone trying to read his own body. She had him in bio. She had watched him argue with his quiz grade for five minutes after class on Monday, polite and stubborn at once, and she had thought then that he was either an egoist about his own reasoning or genuinely trying to understand, and she still couldn't tell which, and she liked that she couldn't tell.

"Ms. Kang says that's lactate," she said. "The burn. When your muscle cells run low on oxygen, they turn pyruvate into lactate." Joshua straightened up. "Pyruvate," he repeated. "That's the middle step. That's in my list." "Then your list is finally useful for something." Ireland took a long drink of her water without asking and she let him, which she considered an altruistic act she would mention later.

Joshua stood in the field with his hands on his knees and his legs still humming, and the list rearranged itself without his permission. The split had to keep going. That was the point he'd been missing, that glycolysis wasn't a hallway to the mitochondria but a machine that had to run, and if the burn meant the cell was trading pyruvate for something so the machine never stopped, then two ATP wasn't a failure, it was what you got when you had nothing else. "It buys back the NAD plus," he said slowly. "The lactate. It regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can keep going, two ATP per glucose, even with no oxygen." He wasn't sure he was saying it right. He was sure his legs were telling him it was true, which felt like a different kind of knowing than the quiz had.

"Is that on the retake?" Isabelle asked. "Everything's on the retake." Ireland was already stretching, one heel hooked on the gate's lower rail. "One more," he said. "From the gate back to the trees. And this time, don't die." Joshua looked down the field, at the grass and the far shade line, and wiped his palms on his shorts. "Two ATP," he said. "Let's go."

story:
The basement smelled of damp carpet and microwave popcorn, and the only light came from two laptops and a strip of bulbs behind the washing machine whose glow turned everyone's hands faintly blue. Edouard had claimed the sagging couch, Gloria sat cross-legged on the rug with her back against the dryer, and Maelle paced between them, reading lines of code over their shoulders like a security guard who distrusted everyone equally. The assignment was due at midnight, and Mr. Lin had been specific on Friday: build a Java class with private fields, expose them only through getter methods, and write tests proving it worked. Edouard's class had worked an hour ago. Now it didn't, and he didn't know why.

"Run it again," Gloria said, without looking up from her own screen.

"I've run it four times. It's not going to suddenly develop a conscience."

Maelle leaned in, close enough that he could hear her breathing. "Your test file. Show me your test file." She read it the way she read everything, top to bottom, mouth slightly open. Then she tapped the screen. "There. That line. You're constructing a BankAccount with no arguments."

"So? That's how I wrote it the first time. It passed then." He said it with more heat than he meant to, because an hour ago the test had passed, green and certain, and now the compiler refused to even look at the rest of his work. The red message sat at the top of the screen like an accusation. Gloria turned her laptop toward him without a word, showing her own identical error, and that was stranger still, because she had copied his structure deliberately, the way she always did, arguing that his naming conventions were the only ones she trusted.

He thought of the summer before, the July his father spent retiling the bathroom. His father had a rule about renovation: never open a wall unless you know what's behind it, because once you open it, everything you uncover becomes your responsibility. Edouard, fourteen and garrulous that whole summer, had asked a hundred questions through the dust, and his father had answered almost none of them, just kept working, until one evening over dinner he said, "The house was fine before you touched it. The question is what you owe it now." Edouard hadn't understood then. Sitting on the couch with the error glowing, he began to.

"Wait," Maelle said slowly. "What did you change? Between the version that passed and this one. There has to be a change."

"The fields. I made them private, like Mr. Lin wanted. And then I wrote a constructor that takes the account number and the balance and sets them. That's the whole difference." He scrolled to show her, and the constructor sat there, plain and legal, four lines long, taking two parameters and assigning them to the private fields. It was clean. It was correct. It was, he was increasingly certain, the reason everything had burned down, and he could not hold both of those beliefs at once.

Gloria had gone very still on the rug. She was the quiet one of the three, the one whose silences usually meant she was two steps ahead, and Edouard watched her face instead of his screen while Maelle clicked through his history. "Here," Maelle said. "Old version. No constructor at all. Just fields and getters. And the test passed."

"Because the compiler adds one for you," Gloria said. She said it to the carpet, quietly, as if reporting something she'd read at three in the morning. "If your class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default no-argument one. But once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added." The words landed in the basement and nobody moved. Edouard read his error message again and it had changed shape entirely, had become almost polite, pointing at the empty parentheses in his test where an account number and a balance were supposed to go. His test wasn't broken. His test was asking for a door that no longer existed.

For a moment he sat there in the blue half-light, feeling two things at no consonance at all: the flat embarrassment of having blamed the compiler, the laptop, Gloria's copy, anything but himself, and underneath it something closer to respect. The language hadn't betrayed him. The language had done exactly what it always did, and if he had known the rule, he would have written the test differently from the start. His old habit was to treat an error as a wall, something to bash against until it surrendered. His father would have said the wall was load-bearing. You could complain about it, or you could ask what it was holding up.

"Fix the test," he said. "Pass the arguments. That's it." He was already typing, changing the empty parentheses to hold an account number and a balance, and Maelle crouched beside him with her hand hovering over the enter key, not touching it, the way you hover at a door you've never opened before. Gloria pulled her own laptop close and fixed her identical line without a word. The strip of lights buzzed. Somewhere upstairs a dishwasher clicked into its rinse cycle. Edouard pressed run, and the three of them watched the output build line by line.
